entries.ed48d4dffa761cc147e9474ab7eaf60d9c091429: <div sID="gen2972" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Num.15" sID="Num.15"/> <div eID="gen2972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2973" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2974" type="x-p"/> This chapter, which is mostly concerning sacrifice and offering, comes in between the story of two rebellions (one <reference osisRef="Num.14.1-Num.14.45">ch. xiv.</reference> the other <reference osisRef="Num.16.1-Num.16.50">ch. xvi.</reference>), to signify that these legal institutions were typical of the gifts which Christ was to receive even for the rebellious, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>. In the foregoing chapter, upon Israel's provocation, God had determined to destroy them, and in token of his wrath had sentenced them to perish in the wilderness. But, upon Moses' intercession, he said, "I have pardoned;" and, in token of that mercy, in this chapter he repeats and explains some of the laws concerning offerings, to show that he was reconciled to them, notwithstanding the severe dispensation they were under, and would not unchurch them. Here is, I. The law concerning the meat-offerings and drink-offerings (<reference osisRef="Num.15.1-Num.15.12">ver. 1-12</reference>) both for Israelites and for strangers (<reference osisRef="Num.15.13-Num.15.16">ver. 13-16</reference>), and a law concerning the heave-offerings of the first of their dough, <reference osisRef="Num.15.17-Num.15.21">ver. 17-21</reference>. II. The law concerning sacrifices for sins of ignorance, <reference osisRef="Num.15.22-Num.15.29">ver. 22-29</reference>. III. The punishment of presumptuous sins (<reference osisRef="Num.15.30-Num.15.31">ver. 30, 31</reference>), and an instance given in the sabbath-breaker, <reference osisRef="Num.15.32-Num.15.36">ver. 32-36</reference>. IV. A law concerning fringes, for memorandums, upon the borders of their garments, <reference osisRef="Num.15.37-Num.15.41">ver. 37</reference>, &c.
entries.54a62906af1ba7c99076740e27e646ad00cdd17c: <div eID="gen2974" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2973" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Laws Concerning Sacrifices. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2975" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye be come into the land of your habitations, which I give unto you, <hi type="super">3</hi> And will make an offering by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , a burnt offering, or a sacrifice in performing a vow, or in a freewill offering, or in your solemn feasts, to make a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , of the herd, or of the flock: <hi type="super">4</hi> Then shall he that offereth his offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> bring a meat offering of a tenth deal of flour mingled with the fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin of oil. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin of wine for a drink offering shalt thou prepare with the burnt offering or sacrifice, for one lamb. <hi type="super">6</hi> Or for a ram, thou shalt prepare <hi type="italic">for</hi> a meat offering two tenth deals of flour mingled with the third <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin of oil. <hi type="super">7</hi> And for a drink offering thou shalt offer the third <hi type="italic">part</hi> of an hin of wine, <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> And when thou preparest a bullock <hi type="italic">for</hi> a burnt offering, or <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sacrifice in performing a vow, or peace offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">9</hi> Then shall he bring with a bullock a meat offering of three tenth deals of flour mingled with half an hin of oil. <hi type="super">10</hi> And thou shalt bring for a drink offering half an hin of wine, <hi type="italic">for</hi> an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 11 Thus shall it be done for one bullock, or for one ram, or for a lamb, or a kid. <hi type="super">12</hi> According to the number that ye shall prepare, so shall ye do to every one according to their number. <hi type="super">13</hi> All that are born of the country shall do these things after this manner, in offering an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> And if a stranger sojourn with you, or whosoever <hi type="italic">be</hi> among you in your generations, and will offer an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; as ye do, so he shall do. <hi type="super">15</hi> One ordinance <hi type="italic">shall be both</hi> for you of the congregation, and also for the stranger that sojourneth <hi type="italic">with you,</hi> an ordinance for ever in your generations: as ye <hi type="italic">are,</hi> so shall the stranger be before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> One law and one manner shall be for you, and for the stranger that sojourneth with you. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye come into the land whither I bring you, 19 Then it shall be, that, when ye eat of the bread of the land, ye shall offer up an heave offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">20</hi> Ye shall offer up a cake of the first of your dough <hi type="italic">for</hi> an heave offering: as <hi type="italic">ye do</hi> the heave offering of the threshingfloor, so shall ye heave it. 21 Of the first of your dough ye shall give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> an heave offering in your generations. <div eID="gen2975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2976" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen2976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2977" type="x-p"/> I. Full instructions given concerning the meat-offerings and drink-offerings, which were appendages to all the sacrifices of animals. The beginning of this law is very encouraging: <hi type="italic">When you come into the land of your habitation which I give unto you,</hi> they you shall do so and so, <reference osisRef="Num.15.2">v. 2</reference>. This was a plain intimation, not only that God was reconciled to them notwithstanding the sentence he had passed upon them, but that he would secure the promised land to their seed notwithstanding their proneness to rebel against him. They might think some time or other they should be guilty of a misdemeanour that would be fatal to them, and would exclude them for ever, as the last had done for one generation; but this intimates an assurance that they should be kept from provoking God to such a degree as would amount to a forfeiture; for this statute takes it for granted that there were some of them that should in due time come into Canaan. The meat-offerings were of two sorts; some were offered alone, and we have the law concerning those, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1-Lev.2.16">Lev. ii. 1</reference>, &c. Others were added to the burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, and constantly attended them, and about these direction is here given. It was requisite, since the sacrifices of acknowledgment (specified in <reference osisRef="Num.15.3">v. 3</reference>) were intended as the food of God's table, that there should be a constant provision of bread, oil, and wine, whatever the flesh-meat was. The caterers or purveyors for Solomon's temple provided <hi type="italic">fine flour,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.22">1 Kings iv. 22</reference>. And it was fit that God should keep a good house, that his table should be furnished with bread as well as flesh, and that his cup should run over. In my Father's house there is bread enough. Now the intent of this law is to direct what proportion the meat-offering and drink-offering should bear to several sacrifices to which they were annexed. If the sacrifice was a lamb or a kid, then the meat-offering must be a tenth-deal of flour, that is, an omer, which contained about five pints; this must be mingled with oil, the fourth part of a hin (a hin contained about five quarts), and the drink-offering must be the same quantity of wine, about a quart and half a pint, <reference osisRef="Num.15.3-Num.15.5">v. 3-5</reference>. If it was a ram, the meat-offering was doubled, two tenth-deals of flour, about five quarts, and a third part of a hin of oil (which was to them as butter is to us) mingled with it; and the same quantity of wine for a drink-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.15.6-Num.15.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. If the sacrifice was a bullock, the meat-offering was to be trebled, three omers, with five pints of oil, and the same quantity of wine for a drink-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.15.8-Num.15.10">v. 8-10</reference>. And thus for each sacrifice, whether offered by a particular person or at the common charge. Note, Our religious services should be governed, as by other rules, so by the rule of proportion. <div eID="gen2977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2978" type="x-p"/> II. Natives and strangers are here set upon a level, in this as in other matters (<reference osisRef="Num.15.13-Num.15.16">v. 13-16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">One law shall be for you and for the stranger</hi> that is proselyted to the Jewish religion." Now, 1. This was an invitation to the Gentiles to become proselytes, and to embrace the faith and worship of the true God. In civil things there was a difference between strangers and true-born Israelites, but not in the things of God; <hi type="italic">as you are, so shall the stranger be before the Lord,</hi> for with him there is no respect of persons. See <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Isa. lvi. 3</reference>. 2. This was an obligation upon the Jews to be kind to strangers, and not to oppress them, because they saw them owned and accepted of God. Communion in religion is a great engagement to mutual affection, and should slay all enmities. 3. It was a mortification to the pride of the Jews, who are apt to be puffed up with their birthright privileges. "We are Abraham's seed." God let them know that the sons of the stranger were as welcome to him as the sons of Jacob; no man's birth or parentage shall turn either to his advantage or his prejudice in his acceptance with God. This likewise intimated that, as believing strangers should be accounted Israelites, so unbelieving Israelites should be accounted strangers. 4. It was a happy presage of the calling of the Gentiles, and of their admission into the church. If the law made so little difference between Jew and Gentile, much less would the gospel make, which broke down the partition-wall, and reconciled both to God in one sacrifice, without the observance of the legal ceremonies. <div eID="gen2978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2979" type="x-p"/> III. A law for the offering of the first of their dough unto the Lord. This, as the former, goes upon the comfortable supposition of their having <hi type="italic">come into the promised land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.15.18">v. 18</reference>. Now that they lived upon manna they needed not such an express acknowledgment of God's title to their daily bread, and their dependence upon him for it, the thing spoke for itself; but in Canaan, where they should eat the fruit of their own industry, God required that he should be owned as their landlord and their great benefactor. They must not only offer him the first-fruits and tenths of the corn in their fields (these had already been reserved); but when they had it in their houses, in their kneading trough, when it was almost ready to be set upon their tables, God must have a further tribute of acknowledgment, part of their dough (the Jews say a fortieth part, at least, of the whole lump) must be heaved or offered up to God (<reference osisRef="Num.15.20-Num.15.21">v. 20, 21</reference>), and the priest must have it for the use of his family. Thus they must own their dependence upon God for their daily bread, even when they had it in the house with them; they must then wait on God for the comfortable use of it; for we read of that which was brought home, and yet God did blow upon it, and it came to little, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">Hag. i. 9</reference>. Christ has taught us to pray not, <hi type="italic">Give us this year our yearly harvest,</hi> but <hi type="italic">Give us this day our daily bread.</hi> God by this law said to the people, as the prophet long afterwards said to the widow of Sarepta (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.13">1 Kings xvii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Only make me thereof a little cake first.</hi> This offering was expressly kept up by the laws of Ezekiel's visionary temple, and it is a commandment with promise of family-mercies (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.30">Ezek. xliv. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall give unto the priest the first of your dough, that he may cause the blessing to rest in thy house;</hi> for, when God has had his dues out of our estates, we may expect the comfort of what falls to our share.
entries.cd4b2478ed4fc7809e4658c1e86c3be3d9e41e93: <div eID="gen2979" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sacrifices for Sins of Ignorance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2980" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And if ye have erred, and not observed all these commandments, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken unto Moses, <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">Even</hi> all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath commanded you by the hand of Moses, from the day that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded <hi type="italic">Moses,</hi> and henceforward among your generations; 24 Then it shall be, if <hi type="italic">ought</hi> be committed by ignorance without the knowledge of the congregation, that all the congregation shall offer one young bullock for a burnt offering, for a sweet savour unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , with his meat offering, and his drink offering, according to the manner, and one kid of the goats for a sin offering. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the priest shall make an atonement for all the congregation of the children of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them; for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> ignorance: and they shall bring their offering, a sacrifice made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and their sin offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , for their ignorance: <hi type="super">26</hi> And it shall be forgiven all the congregation of the children of Israel, and the stranger that sojourneth among them; seeing all the people <hi type="italic">were</hi> in ignorance. <hi type="super">27</hi> And if any soul sin through ignorance, then he shall bring a she goat of the first year for a sin offering. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the priest shall make an atonement for the soul that sinneth ignorantly, when he sinneth by ignorance before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to make an atonement for him; and it shall be forgiven him. <hi type="super">29</hi> Ye shall have one law for him that sinneth through ignorance, <hi type="italic">both for</hi> him that is born among the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them. <div eID="gen2980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2981" type="x-p"/> We have here the laws concerning sacrifices for sins of ignorance; the Jews understand it of idolatry, or false worship, through the error of their teachers. The case here supposed is that they <hi type="italic">had not observed all these commandments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.15.22-Num.15.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. If they had failed in the offerings of their acknowledgment, and had not brought them according to the law, then they must bring an offering of atonement, yea, though the omission had been through forgetfulness or mistake. If they failed in one part of the ceremony, they must make it up by the observance of another part, which was in the nature of a remedial law. 1. The case is put of a national sin, committed through ignorance, and become customary through a vulgar error (<reference osisRef="Num.15.24">v. 24</reference>)—<hi type="italic">the congregation,</hi> that is, the body of the people, for so it is explained (<reference osisRef="Num.15.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the congregation of the children of Israel.</hi> The ceremonial observances were so numerous, and so various, that, it might easily be supposed, some of them by degrees would be forgotten and disused, as particularly that immediately before concerning the heave-offering of their dough: now if, in process of time, upon consulting the law, there should appear to have been a general neglect of that or any other appointment, then a sacrifice must be offered for the whole congregation, and the oversight shall be forgiven (<reference osisRef="Num.15.25-Num.15.26">v. 25, 26</reference>) and not punished, as it deserved, with some national judgment. The offering of the sacrifice <hi type="italic">according to the manner,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ordinance,</hi> plainly refers to a former statute, of which this is the repetition; and the same bullock which is there called <hi type="italic">a sin-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.13">Lev. iv. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.21">21</reference>) is here called <hi type="italic">a burnt-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.15.24">v. 24</reference>), because it was wholly burnt, though not upon the altar, yet without the camp. And here is the addition of a <hi type="italic">kid of the goats for a sin-offering.</hi> According to this law, we find that Hezekiah made atonement for the errors of his father's reign, by <hi type="italic">seven bullocks, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven he-goats,</hi> which he offered as a <hi type="italic">sin-offering for the kingdom, and for the sanctuary, and for Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.21">2 Chron. xxix. 21</reference>), and <hi type="italic">for all Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.15.24">v. 24</reference>. And we find the like done after the return out of captivity, <reference osisRef="Ezra.8.35">Ezra viii. 35</reference>. 2. It is likewise supposed to be the case of a particular person: <hi type="italic">If any soul sin through ignorance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.15.27">v. 27</reference>), neglecting any part of his duty, he must bring his offering, as was appointed, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.27-Lev.4.35">Lev. iv. 27</reference>, &c. Thus atonement shall be made <hi type="italic">for the soul that sins, when he sins through ignorance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.15.28">v. 28</reference>. Observe, (1.) Sins committed ignorantly need to have atonement made for them; for, though ignorance will in a degree excuse, it will not justify those that might have known their Lord's will and did it not. David prayed to be cleansed from his <hi type="italic">secret faults,</hi> that is, those sins which he himself was not aware of, the errors he did not understand, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.12">Ps. xix. 12</reference>. (2.) Sins committed ignorantly shall be forgiven, through Christ the great sacrifice, who, when he offered up himself once for all upon the cross, seemed to explain the intention of his offering in that prayer, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.</hi> And Paul seems to allude to this law concerning sins of ignorance (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1 Tim. i. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly and in unbelief.</hi> And it looked favourable upon the Gentiles that this law of atoning for sins of ignorance is expressly made to extend to those who were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel (<reference osisRef="Num.15.29">v. 29</reference>), but supposed to be <hi type="italic">proselytes of righteousness.</hi> Thus the blessing of Abraham comes upon the Gentiles.
entries.9d69bd17571a6f46310365d2c0679f0cd7de75ab: <div eID="gen2981" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Doom of Presumptuous Sinners. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2982" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> But the soul that doeth <hi type="italic">ought</hi> presumptuously, <hi type="italic">whether he be</hi> born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people. <hi type="super">31</hi> Because he hath despised the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and hath broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off; his iniquity <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon him. <hi type="super">32</hi> And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they that found him gathering sticks brought him unto Moses and Aaron, and unto all the congregation. <hi type="super">34</hi> And they put him in ward, because it was not declared what should be done to him. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, The man shall be surely put to death: all the congregation shall stone him with stones without the camp. <hi type="super">36</hi> And all the congregation brought him without the camp, and stoned him with stones, and he died; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <div eID="gen2982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2983" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The general doom passed upon presumptuous sinners. 1. Those are to be reckoned presumptuous sinners that sin <hi type="italic">with a high hand,</hi> as the original phrase is (<reference osisRef="Num.15.30">v. 30</reference>), that is, that avowedly confront God's authority, and set up their own lust in competition with it, that sin for sinning-sake, in contradiction to the precept of the law, and in defiance of the penalty, that fight against God, and dare him to do his worst; see <reference osisRef="Job.15.25">Job xv. 25</reference>. It is not only to sin against knowledge, but to sin designedly against God's will and glory. 2. Sins thus committed are exceedingly sinful. He that thus breaks the commandment, (1.) <hi type="italic">Reproaches the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.15.30">v. 30</reference>); he says the worst he can of him, and most unjustly. The language of presumptuous sin is, "Eternal truth is not fit to be believed, the Lord of all not fit to be obeyed, and almighty power not fit to be either feared or trusted." It imputes folly to Infinite Wisdom, and iniquity to the righteous Judge of heaven and earth; such is the malignity of wilful sin. (2.) He <hi type="italic">despises the word of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.15.31">v. 31</reference>. There are those who, in many instances, come short of fulfilling the word, and yet have a great value for it, and count the law honourable; but presumptuous sinners despise it, thinking themselves too great, too good, and too wise, to be ruled by it. <hi type="italic">What is the Almighty that we should serve him?</hi> Whatever the sin itself is, it is contumacy that incurs the anathema. It is rebellion added to the sin that is as witch-craft, and stubbornness as idolatry. 3. The sentence passed on such is dreadful. There remains no sacrifice for those sins; the law provided none: <hi type="italic">That soul shall be cut off from among his people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.15.30">v. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">utterly cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.15.31">v. 31</reference>); and that God may be for ever justified, and the sinner for ever confounded, <hi type="italic">his iniquity shall be upon him,</hi> and there needs no more to sink him to the lowest hell. Thus the Jewish doctors understand it, that <hi type="italic">the iniquity shall cleave to the soul, after it is cut off, and that man shall give an account of his sin at the great day of judgment.</hi> Perhaps the kind of offence might be such as did not expose the offender to the censure of the civil magistrate, but, if it was done presumptuously, God himself would take the punishment of it into his own hands, and into them it is a fearful thing to fall. In the New Testament we find the like sentence of exclusion from all benefit by the great sacrifice passed upon the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, and a total apostasy from Christianity. <div eID="gen2983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2984" type="x-p"/> II. A particular instance of presumption in the sin of sabbath-breaking. 1. The offence was the gathering of sticks on the sabbath day (<reference osisRef="Num.15.32">v. 32</reference>), which, it is probable, were designed to make a fire of, whereas they were commanded to bake and seeth what they had occasion for the day before, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.23">Exod. xvi. 23</reference>. This seemed but a small offence, but it was a violation of the law of the sabbath, and so was a tacit contempt of the Creator, to whose honour the sabbath was dedicated, and an incursion upon the whole law, which the sabbath was intended as a hedge about. And it appears by the context to have been done presumptuously, and in affront both of the law and to the Law-maker. 2. The offender was secured, <reference osisRef="Num.15.33-Num.15.34">v. 33, 34</reference>. Those that found him <hi type="italic">gathering sticks,</hi> in their zeal for the honour of the sabbath, <hi type="italic">brought him to Moses and Aaron, and all the congregation,</hi> which intimates that being the sabbath day the congregation was at that time gathered to Moses and Aaron, to receive instruction from them, and to join with them in religious worship. It seems, even common Israelites, though there was much amiss among them, yet would not contentedly see the sabbath profaned, which was a good sign that they had not quite forsaken God, nor were utterly forsaken of him. 3. God was consulted, <hi type="italic">because it was not declared what should be done to him.</hi> The law had already made the profanation of the sabbath a capital crime (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.14">Exod. xxxi. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.35.2">ch. xxxv. 2</reference>); but they were in doubt, either concerning the offence (whether this that he had done should be deemed a profanation or no) or concerning the punishment, which death he should die. God was the Judge, and before him they brought this cause. 4. Sentence was passed; the prisoner was adjudged a sabbath-breaker, according to the intent of that law, and as such he must be put to death; and to show how great the crime was, and how displeasing to God, and that others might hear and fear and not do in like manner presumptuously, that death is appointed him which was looked upon as most terrible: He must be <hi type="italic">stoned with stones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.15.35">v. 35</reference>. Note, God is jealous for the honour of his sabbaths, and will not hold those guiltless, whatever men do, that profane them. 5. Execution was done pursuant to the sentence, <reference osisRef="Num.15.36">v. 36</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">stoned</hi> to death <hi type="italic">by the congregation.</hi> As many as could were employed in the execution, that those, at least, might be afraid of breaking the sabbath, who had thrown a stone at this sabbath-breaker. This intimates that the open profanation of the sabbath is a sin which ought to be punished and restrained by the civil magistrate, who, as far as overt acts go, is keeper of both tables. See <reference osisRef="Neh.13.17">Neh. xiii. 17</reference>. One would think there could be no great harm in gathering a few sticks, on what day soever it was, but God intended the exemplary punishment of him that did so for a standing warning to us all, to make conscience of keeping holy the sabbath.
entries.33c6e1b73bd44cf34b3ff0c9d49c4cf69e58c010: <div eID="gen2984" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Law Concerning Fringes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2985" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">38</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue: <hi type="super">39</hi> And it shall be unto you for a fringe, that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring: <hi type="super">40</hi> That ye may remember, and do all my commandments, and be holy unto your God. 41 I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt, to be your God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <div eID="gen2985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2986" type="x-p"/> Provision had been just now made by the law for the pardon of sins of ignorance and infirmity; now here is an expedient provided for the preventing of such sins. They are ordered to make fringes upon the borders of their garments, which were to be memorandums to them of their duty, that they might not sin through forgetfulness. 1. The sign appointed is a fringe of silk, or thread, or worsted, or the garment itself ravelled at the bottom, and a blue riband bound on the top of it to keep it tight, <reference osisRef="Num.15.38">v. 38</reference>. The Jews being a peculiar people, they were thus distinguished from their neighbours in their dress, as well as in their diet, and taught by such little instances of singularity not to be conformed to the way of the heathen in greater things. Thus likewise they proclaimed themselves Jews wherever they were, as those that were not ashamed of God and his law. Our Saviour, being made under the law, wore these fringes; hence we read of the hem or border, of his garment, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.20">Matt. ix. 20</reference>. These borders the Pharisees enlarged, that they might be thought more holy and devout than other people. The phylacteries were different things; these were their own invention, the fringes were a divine institution. The Jews at this day wear them, saying, when they put them on, <hi type="italic">Blessed be he who has sanctified us unto himself, and commanded us to wear fringes.</hi> 2. The intention of it was to remind them that they were a peculiar people. They were not appointed for the trimming and adorning of their clothes, but <hi type="italic">to stir up their pure minds by way of remembrance</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.1">2 Pet. iii. 1</reference>), that they might <hi type="italic">look upon the fringe and remember the commandments.</hi> Many look upon their ornaments to feed their pride, but they must look upon these ornaments to awaken their consciences to a sense of their duty, that their religion might constantly beset them, and that they might carry it about with them, as they did their clothes, wherever they went. If they were tempted to sin, the fringe would be a monitor to them not to break God's commandments: If a duty was forgotten to be done in its season, the fringe would remind them of it. This institution, though it is not an imposition upon us, is an instruction to us, always to <hi type="italic">remember the commandments of the Lord our God,</hi> that we <hi type="italic">may do them,</hi> to treasure them up in our memories, and to apply them to particular cases as there is occasion to use them. It was intended particularly to be a preservative from idolatry: that you <hi type="italic">seek not after your own heart, and your own eyes,</hi> in your religious worship. Yet it may extend also to the whole conversation, for nothing is more contrary to God's honour, and our own true interest, than to <hi type="italic">walk in the way of our heart</hi> and in <hi type="italic">the sight of our eyes;</hi> for the <hi type="italic">imagination of the heart is evil,</hi> and so is the <hi type="italic">lust of the eyes.</hi> <div eID="gen2986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2987" type="x-p"/> After the repetition of some ceremonial appointments, the chapter closes with that great and fundamental law of religion, <hi type="italic">Be holy unto your God,</hi> purged from sin, and sincerely devoted to his service; and that great reason for all the commandments is again and again inculcated, <hi type="italic">I am the Lord your God.</hi> Did we more firmly believe, and more frequently and seriously consider, that God is the Lord, and our God and Redeemer, we should see ourselves bound in duty, interest, and gratitude, to keep all his commandments.  <chapter eID="Num.15"/> <div eID="gen2987" type="x-p"/>

entries.30574e1fc539915ff5fde58d89194158fbf17851: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1391"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.15.1-Num.15.41">Nu 15:1-41</reference>. The Law of Sundry Offerings.</title> <div sID="gen1878" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1391"/><hi type="bold">1-2. The Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel--</hi>Some infer from <reference osisRef="Num.15.23">Nu 15:23</reference> that the date of this communication must be fixed towards the close of the wanderings in the wilderness; and, also, that all the sacrifices prescribed in the law were to be offered only after the settlement in Canaan. <div eID="gen1878" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a6c59d76a0e0e62856866541b1394ddc1e95c09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1392"/><div sID="gen1879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1392"/><hi type="bold">3. make an offering by fire unto the Lord, a burnt offering--</hi>It is evident that a peace offering is referred to because this term is frequently used in such a sense (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.12">Ex 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.17.5">Le 17:5</reference>). <div eID="gen1879" type="x-p"/>
entries.b29390caac425f927a8ed7bb16792d5556097295: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1393"/><div sID="gen1880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1393"/><hi type="bold">4. tenth deal--</hi>that is, an omer, the tenth part of an ephah (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.36">Ex 16:36</reference>).<div eID="gen1880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fourth part of an hin of oil--</hi>This element shows it to have been different from such meat offerings as were made by themselves, and not merely accompaniments of other sacrifices. <div eID="gen1881" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cfcab693608c6497442a69c81c90241879a4827: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1394"/><div sID="gen1882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1394"/><hi type="bold">6-12. two tenth deals--</hi>The quantity of flour was increased because the sacrifice was of superior value to the former. The accessory sacrifices were always increased in proportion to the greater worth and magnitude of its principal. <div eID="gen1882" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc0a1cb2abbfebeef7444148a6bb0c8217d5f9a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1395"/><div sID="gen1883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1395"/><hi type="bold">13-16. a stranger--</hi>one who had become a proselyte. There were scarcely any of the national privileges of the Israelites, in which the Gentile stranger might not, on conforming to certain conditions, fully participate. <div eID="gen1883" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a51f5295433b48b19c8da2a6de8ce5027e737f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1396"/><div sID="gen1884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1396"/><hi type="bold">19. when ye eat of the bread of the land, ye shall offer up an heave offering--</hi>The offering prescribed was to precede the act of eating.<div eID="gen1884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the Lord--</hi>that is, the priests of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.30">Eze 44:30</reference>). <div eID="gen1885" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe6c4f2280088d2eb9f2e861e1fe169d1adf618b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1397"/><div sID="gen1886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1397"/><hi type="bold">20. heave offering of the threshing-floor--</hi>meaning the corn on the threshing-floor; that is, after harvest.<div eID="gen1886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so shall ye heave it--</hi>to the priests accompanying the ceremony with the same rites. <div eID="gen1887" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf03845a342850cc47403ef7c006ff8086156579: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1398"/><div sID="gen1888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1398"/><hi type="bold">22. if ye have erred, and not observed all these commandments, &c.--</hi>respecting the performance of divine worship, and the rites and ceremonies that constitute the holy service. The law relates only to any omission and consequently is quite different from that laid down in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13">Le 4:13</reference>, which implies a transgression or positive neglect of some observances required. This law relates to private parties or individual tribes; that to the whole congregation of Israel. <div eID="gen1888" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae1d21ba0abca3af23deaf6f937f1cdd7e9958a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1399"/><div sID="gen1889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1399"/><hi type="bold">24-26. if aught be committed by ignorance--</hi>The Mosaic ritual was complicated, and the ceremonies to be gone through in the various instances of purification which are specified, would expose a worshipper, through ignorance, to the risk of omitting or neglecting some of them. This law includes the stranger in the number of those for whom the sacrifice was offered for the sin of general ignorance. <div eID="gen1889" type="x-p"/>
entries.3098025dec6d4c5ff2ab4c7087e44e44d63194a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1400"/><div sID="gen1890" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1400"/><hi type="bold">27-29. if any soul sin through ignorance--</hi>not only in common with the general body of the people, but his personal sins were to be expiated in the same manner. <div eID="gen1890" type="x-p"/>
entries.882c36cbb142d52794e18a9c7855e924e8f718db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1401"/><div sID="gen1891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1401"/><hi type="bold">30. the soul that doeth aught presumptuously--</hi>Hebrew, "with an high" or "uplifted hand"--that is, knowingly, wilfully, obstinately. In this sense the phraseology occurs (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.8">Ex 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">Le 26:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">Psa 19:13</reference>).<div eID="gen1891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same reproacheth the Lord--</hi>sets Him at open defiance and dishonors His majesty. <div eID="gen1892" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bda2f79b47206ae4240af2163440c40a6e0e352: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1402"/><div sID="gen1893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1402"/><hi type="bold">31. his iniquity shall be upon him--</hi>The punishment of his sins shall fall on himself individually; no guilt shall be incurred by the nation, unless there be a criminal carelessness in overlooking the offense. <div eID="gen1893" type="x-p"/>
entries.36232411e6efdd718f189cd2f5a1deb6aa3dd753: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1403"/><div sID="gen1894" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1403"/><hi type="bold">32-34. a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day--</hi>This incident is evidently narrated as an instance of presumptuous sin. The mere gathering of sticks was not a sinful act and might be necessary for fuel to warm him or to make ready his food. But its being done on the Sabbath altered the entire character of the action. The law of the Sabbath being a plain and positive commandment, this transgression of it was a known and wilful sin, and it was marked by several aggravations. For the deed was done with unblushing boldness in broad daylight, in open defiance of the divine authority--in flagrant inconsistency with His religious connection with Israel, as the covenant-people of God; and it was an application to improper purposes of time, which God had consecrated to Himself and the solemn duties of religion. The offender was brought before the rulers, who, on hearing the painful report, were at a loss to determine what ought to be done. That they should have felt any embarrassment in such a case may seem surprising, in the face of the sabbath law (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.14">Ex 31:14</reference>). Their difficulty probably arose from this being the first public offense of the kind which had occurred; and the appeal might be made to remove all ground of complaint--to produce a more striking effect, so that the fate of this criminal might be a beacon to warn all Israelites in the future. <div eID="gen1894" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dfe77f72849bf2d9c04cd1e3163b1ffa2de9d67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1404"/><div sID="gen1895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1404"/><hi type="bold">35-36. The Lord said unto Moses, The man shall be surely put to death--</hi>The Lord was King, as well as God of Israel, and the offense being a violation of the law of the realm, the Sovereign Judge gave orders that this man should be put to death; and, moreover, He required the whole congregation unite in executing the fatal sentence. <div eID="gen1895" type="x-p"/>
entries.e006323730e158adfeffa53622a32d89fc032f07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1405"/><div sID="gen1896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1405"/><hi type="bold">38. bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments--</hi>These were narrow strips, in a wing-like form, wrapped over the shoulders and on various parts of the attire. "Fringe," however, is the English rendering of two distinct Hebrew words--the one meaning a narrow lappet or edging, called the "hem" or "border" (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.5">Mt 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.44">Lu 8:44</reference>), which, in order to make it more attractive to the eye and consequently more serviceable to the purpose described, was covered with a riband of blue or rather purple color; the other term signifies strings with tassels at the end, fastened to the corners of the garment. Both of these are seen on the Egyptian and Assyrian frocks; and as the Jewish people were commanded by express and repeated ordinances to have them, the fashion was rendered subservient, in their case, to awaken high and religious associations--to keep them in habitual remembrance of the divine commandments. <div eID="gen1896" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a5fdacb5faa1abc75227a5a215d399528bdc1aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1406"/><div sID="gen1897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1406"/><hi type="bold">41. I am the Lord your God--</hi>The import of this solemn conclusion is, that though He was displeased with them for their frequent rebellions, for which they would be doomed to forty years' wanderings, He would not abandon them but continue His divine protection and care of them till they were brought into the land of promise. <chapter eID="Num.15"/>

entries.325a4d3a59058a063e410cdb1174ccdd5a64a9ac: <div eID="gen5602" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5603" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5604" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5604" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5603" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5605" type="x-p"/> Directions concerning the different offerings they should bring unto the Lord when they should come to the land of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Num.15.1-Num.15.3">Num 15:1-3</reference>. Directions relative to the meat-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.15.4">Num 15:4</reference>; to the drink-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.15.5">Num 15:5</reference>. Of the burnt-offering, vow-offering, peace-offering, drink-offering, etc., <reference osisRef="Num.15.6-Num.15.12">Num 15:6-12</reference>. All born in the country must perform these rites, <reference osisRef="Num.15.13">Num 15:13</reference>, and the strangers also, <reference osisRef="Num.15.14-Num.15.16">Num 15:14-16</reference>. They shall offer unto the Lord a heave-offering of the first-fruits of the land, <reference osisRef="Num.15.17-Num.15.21">Num 15:17-21</reference>. Concerning omissions through ignorance, and the sacrifices to be offered on such occasions, <reference osisRef="Num.15.22-Num.15.29">Num 15:22-29</reference>. He who sins presumptuously shall be cut off, <reference osisRef="Num.15.30">Num 15:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.15.31">Num 15:31</reference>. History of the person who gathered sticks on the Sabbath, <reference osisRef="Num.15.32">Num 15:32</reference>. He is brought to Moses and Aaron, <reference osisRef="Num.15.33">Num 15:33</reference>. They put him in confinement till the mind of the Lord should be known on the case, <reference osisRef="Num.15.34">Num 15:34</reference>. The Lord commands him to be stoned, <reference osisRef="Num.15.35">Num 15:35</reference>. He is stoned to death, <reference osisRef="Num.15.36">Num 15:36</reference>. The Israelites are commanded to make fringes to the borders of their garments, <reference osisRef="Num.15.37">Num 15:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.15.38">Num 15:38</reference>. The end for which these fringes were to be made, that they might remember the commandments of the Lord, that they might be holy, <reference osisRef="Num.15.39-Num.15.41">Num 15:39-41</reference>.
entries.20135643bcd79d9fad3422dafe9f6b0231988199: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen5605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5606" type="x-p"/> When ye be come into the land - Some learned men are of opinion that several offerings prescribed by the law were not intended to be made in the wilderness, but in the promised land; the former not affording those conveniences which were necessary to the complete observance of the Divine worship in this and several other respects.
entries.baeb35b3469a13dfa4b27458e73b2730f89597bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5607" type="x-p"/> And will make an offering - For the different kinds of offerings, sacrifices, etc., see <reference osisRef="Lev.1.2">Lev 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.7">Lev 1:7</reference>.
entries.60ce62241df60a37eb066b7548bdae17e815a2b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen5607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5608" type="x-p"/> The fourth part of a hin - The quantity of meal and flour was augmented in proportion to the size of the sacrifice with which it was offered. With a Lamb or a Kid were offered one tenth deal of flour, (the tenth part of an ephah, see on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.40">Exo 29:40</reference> (note)), the fourth part of a hin of oil, and the fourth part of a hin of wine. With a Ram, two tenth deals of flour, a third part of a hin of oil, and a third part of a hin of wine. With a Bullock, three tenth deals of flour, half a hin of oil, and half a hin of wine. See <reference osisRef="Num.15.4-Num.15.11">Num 15:4-11</reference>.
entries.04bdd5bbb5fe6b3cac09d492f1e4183361e11d7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen5608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5609" type="x-p"/> If a stranger sojourn - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.33">Lev 19:33</reference>;<reference osisRef="Lev.22.9">Lev 22:9</reference>. When the case of the Jewish people is fairly considered, and their situation with respect to the surrounding idolatrous nations, we shall see the absolute necessity of having but one form of worship in the land. That alone was genuine which was prescribed by the Almighty, and no others could be tolerated, because they were idolatrous. All strangers - all that came to sojourn in the land, were required to conform to it; and it was right that those who did conform to it should have equal rights and privileges with the Hebrews themselves, which we find was the case. But under the Christian dispensation, as no particular form of worship is prescribed, the types and ceremonies of the Mosaic institution being all fulfilled, unlimited toleration should be allowed; and while the sacred writings are made the basis of the worship offered to God, every man should be allowed to worship according to his own conscience, for in this respect every one is "Lord of himself, accountable to none <div eID="gen5609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5610" type="x-p"/> But to his conscience and his God alone."
entries.9afd8b9388fae9e174c3e157439862dd19fdad7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen5610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5611" type="x-p"/> Ye shall offer - the first of your dough - Concerning the offerings of first-fruits, see the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.22.29">Exo 22:29</reference>.
entries.29508200baaa765e02a0503e0adddf4a2dd4539f: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen5611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5612" type="x-p"/> If aught be committed by ignorance - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.5.17">Lev 5:17</reference>. The case here probably refers to the whole congregation; the cases above, to the sin of an individual.
entries.692ea5341e769b10aff3f784975bff55f81ba63e: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen5612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5613" type="x-p"/> The priest shall make an atonement - Even sins committed through ignorance required an atonement; and God in his mercy has provided one for them.
entries.c989129fb46a0cf1f942575c9b67103b91de34b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen5613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5614" type="x-p"/> But the soul that doeth aught presumptuously - Bold daring acts of transgression against the fullest evidence, and in despite of the Divine authority, admitted of no atonement; the person was to be cut off - to be excluded from God's people, and from all their privileges and blessings. <div eID="gen5614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5615" type="x-p"/> Probably the presumption mentioned here implied an utter contempt of the word and authority of God, springing from an idolatrous or atheistical mind. In such a case all repentance was precluded, because of the denial of the word and being of God. It is probably a case similar to that mentioned <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.8">Heb 6:4-8</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.31">Heb 10:26-31</reference> (note); on which passages see the notes.
entries.645983ca2d864245d69f2b0d87a16b05fd1b1238: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen5615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5616" type="x-p"/> They found a man that gathered sticks upon the Sabbath - This was in all likelihood a case of that kind supposed above: the man despised the word of the Lord, and therefore broke his commandment; see <reference osisRef="Num.15.31">Num 15:31</reference>. On this ground he was punished with the utmost rigor of the law.
entries.f582eccf0204951a6c37313385dbe707a0c5b338: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen5616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5617" type="x-p"/> Stoned him - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.24.23">Lev 24:23</reference>.
entries.b803210d4ec3a3a90ec9eefa6a1279030cc3d51f: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen5617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5618" type="x-p"/> Bid them - make them fringes - We learn from <reference osisRef="Num.15.39">Num 15:39</reference> that these fringes were emblematical of the various commands of God. That there was any analogy between a fringe and a precept, it would be bold to assert; but when a thing is appointed to represent another, no matter how different, that first object be comes the regular representative or sign of the other. There is no analogy between the term bread and the farinaceous nutritive substance thereby signified; but because this term is used to express and represent that thing, every person thus understands it; and when the word bread is seen or heard, a perfect knowledge, not of the letters which compose that word, but of the thing signified by it, is conveyed to the mind. So the fringes, being appointed by God to represent and bring to mind the commandments of God, <reference osisRef="Num.15.39">Num 15:39</reference>, the mention or sight of them conveyed the intelligence intended. All the Jews wore these, and so probably did our Lord; see <reference osisRef="Mat.9.20">Mat 9:20</reference>, where the word κρασπε ον is rather to be understood of the fringe than of the hem of his garment.  <chapter eID="Num.15"/> <div eID="gen5618" type="x-p"/>

entries.418b006a77ac3ecc84330aa7f4bc5b1e51cdd648: Num 15:1-2 <div eID="gen1785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1786" type="x-p"/> Regulations concerning Sacrifices. - Vv. 1-16. For the purpose of reviving the hopes of the new generation that was growing up, and directing their minds to the promised land, during the mournful and barren time when judgment was being executed upon the race that had been condemned, Jehovah communicated various laws through Moses concerning the presentation of sacrifices in the land that He would give them (Num 15:1 and Num 15:2), whereby the former laws of sacrifice were supplemented and completed. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> of these laws had reference to the connection between meat-offerings and drink-offerings on the one hand, and burnt-offerings and slain-offerings on the other.
entries.8a04b4a44bf594f690479e4432d9e7e06aedc380: Num 15:3-5 <div eID="gen1786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1787" type="x-p"/> In the land of Canaan, every burnt and slain-offering, whether prepared in fulfilment of a vow, or spontaneously, or on feast-days (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.22.18">Lev 22:18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.23.38">Lev 23:38</reference>), was to be associated with a meat-offering of fine flour mixed with oil, and a drink-offering of wine, - the quantity to be regulated according to the kind of animal that was slain in sacrifice. (See <reference osisRef="Lev.23.18">Lev 23:18</reference>, where this connection is already mentioned in the case of the festal sacrifices.) For a lamb (כּבשׂ, i.e., either sheep or goat, cf. Num 15:11), they were to take the tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with the quarter of a hin of oil and the quarter of a hin of wine, as a drink-offering. In Num 15:5, the construction changes from the third to the second person. עשׂה, to prepare, as in Exo 29:38.
entries.78a6ab3b75e1c5a0606aa6b0cb899320d1146364: Num 15:6-7 <div eID="gen1787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1788" type="x-p"/> For a ram, they were to take two tenths of fine flour, with the third of a hin of oil and the third of a hin of wine.
entries.bfdb039016fcfbdfefb3af7dae43933ef4a992f1: Num 15:8-10 <div eID="gen1788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1789" type="x-p"/> For an ox, three tenths of fine flour, with half a hin of oil and half a hin of wine. The הקריב (3rd person) in Num 15:9, between תּעשׂה in Num 15:8, and תּקריב in Num 15:10, is certainly striking and unusual, but no so offensive as to render it necessary to alter it into ותּקריב.
entries.365eda2d50869a84934f3865982daff0c92d92e2: Num 15:11-12 <div eID="gen1789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1790" type="x-p"/> The quantities mentioned were to be offered with every ox, or ram, or lamb, of either sheep or goat, and therefore the number of the appointed quantities of meat and drink-offerings was to correspond to the number of sacrificial animals.
entries.0ba13be563a73b6874a9579da4e3eed1a25df0f5: Num 15:13-14 <div eID="gen1790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1791" type="x-p"/> These rules were to apply not only to the sacrifices of those that were born in Israel, but also to those of the strangers living among them. By “these things,” in Num 15:13, we are to understand the meat and drink-offerings already appointed.
entries.803f75de8f917089fad8ed9c4a16a01a0b494a69: Num 15:15-25 <div eID="gen1791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1792" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">As for the assembly, there shall be one law for the Israelite and the stranger,...an eternal ordinance...before Jehovah</hi>.” הקּהל, which is construed absolutely, refers to the assembling of the nation before Jehovah, or to the congregation viewed in its attitude with regard to God. <div eID="gen1792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1793" type="x-p"/> A <hi type="italic">second</hi> law (Num 15:17-21) appoints, on the ground of the general regulations in <reference osisRef="Exod.22.28">Exo 22:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Exo 23:19</reference>, the presentation of a heave-offering from the bread which they would eat in the land of Canaan, viz., a first-fruit of groat-meal (עריסת ראשׁית) baked as cake (חלּה). <hi type="italic">Arisoth</hi>, which is only used in connection with the gift of first-fruits, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.30">Eze 44:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.38">Neh 10:38</reference>, and the passage before us, signifies most probably groats, or meal coarsely bruised, like the talmudical ערסן, <hi type="italic">contusum, mola, far, </hi>and indeed <hi type="italic">far hordei</hi>. This cake of the groats of first-fruits they were to offer “<hi type="italic">as a heave-offering of the threshing-floor,</hi>” i.e., as a heave-offering of the bruised corn, in the same manner as this (therefore, in addition to it, and along with it); and that “<hi type="italic">according to your generations</hi>” (see <reference osisRef="Exod.12.14">Exo 12:14</reference>), that is to say, for all time, to consecrate a gift of first-fruits to the Lord, not only of the grains of corn, but also of the bread made from the corn, and “<hi type="italic">to cause a blessing to rest upon his house</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.30">Eze 44:30</reference>). Like all the gifts of first-fruits, this cake also fell to the portion of the priests (see Ezek. and Neh. <hi type="italic">ut sup</hi>.). <div eID="gen1793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1794" type="x-p"/> To these there are added, in Num 15:22, Num 15:31, laws relating to <hi type="italic">sin-offerings</hi>, the first of which, in Num 15:22-26, is distinguished from the case referred to in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13-Lev.4.21">Lev 4:13-21</reference>, by the fact that the sin is not described here, as it is there, as “doing one of the commandments of Jehovah which ought not to be done,” but as “not doing all that Jehovah had spoken through Moses.” Consequently, the allusion here is not to sins of commission, but to sins of omission, not following the law of God, “<hi type="italic">even</hi> (as is afterwards explained in Num 15:23) all <hi type="italic">that the Lord hath commanded you by the hand of Moses from the day that the Lord hath commanded, and thenceforward according to your generations,</hi>” i.e., since the first beginning of the giving of the law, and during the whole of the time following (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). These words apparently point to a complete falling away of the congregation from the whole of the law. Only the further stipulation in Num 15:24, “<hi type="italic">if it occur away from the eyes of the congregation through error</hi>” (in oversight), cannot be easily reconciled with this, as it seems hardly conceivable that an apostasy from the entire law should have remained hidden from the congregation. This “not doing all the commandments of Jehovah,” of which the congregation is supposed to incur the guilt without perceiving it, might consist either in the fact that, in particular instances, whether from oversight or negligence, the whole congregation omitted to fulfil the commandments of God, i.e., certain precepts of the law, sc., in the fact that they neglected the true and proper fulfilment of the whole law, either, as <hi type="italic">Outram</hi> supposes, “by retaining to a certain extent the national rites, and following the worship of the true God, and yet at the same time acting unconsciously in opposition to the law, through having been led astray by some common errors;” or by allowing the evil example of godless rulers to seduce them to neglect their religious duties, or to adopt and join in certain customs and usages of the heathen, which appeared to be reconcilable with the law of Jehovah, though they really led to contempt and neglect of the commandments of the Lord.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Maimonides</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Outram</hi>, <hi type="italic">ex veterum sententia</hi>) understands this law as relating to extraneous worship; and Outram himself refers to the times of the wicked kings, “when the people neglected their hereditary rites, and, forgetting the sacred laws, fell by a common sin into the observance of the religious rites of other nations.” Undoubtedly, we have historical ground in 2Ch 29:21., and Ezr 8:35, for this interpretation of our law, but further allusions are not excluded in consequence. We cannot agree with <hi type="italic">Baumgarten</hi>, therefore, in restricting the difference between Lev 4:13. and the passage before us to the fact, that the former supposes the transgression of one particular commandment on the part of the whole congregation, whilst the latter (Num 15:22, Num 15:23) refers to a continued lawless condition on the part of Israel.</note> <div eID="gen1794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1795" type="x-p"/> But as a disregard or neglect of the commandments of God had to be expiated, a burnt-offering was to be added to the sin-offering, that the separation of the congregation from the Lord, which had arisen from the sin of omission, might be entirely removed. The apodosis commences with והיה in Num 15:24, but is interrupted by מעי אם, and resumed again with ועשׂוּ, “<hi type="italic">it shall be, if...the whole congregation shall prepare,</hi>” etc. The burnt-offering, being the principal sacrifice, is mentioned as usual before the sin-offering, although, when presented, it followed the latter, on account of its being necessary that the sin should be expiated before the congregation could sanctify its life and efforts afresh to the Lord in the burnt-offering. “<hi type="italic">One kid of the goats:</hi>” see Lev 4:23. כּמּשׂפּט (as in <reference osisRef="Lev.5.10">Lev 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.9.16">Lev 9:16</reference>, etc.) refers to the right established in Num 15:8, Num 15:9, concerning the combination of the meat and drink-offering with the burnt-offering. The sin-offering was to be treated according to the rule laid down in Lev 4:14.
entries.c0e5631e0e43d59af83238d8a77b0823809815f0: Num 15:26 <div eID="gen1795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1796" type="x-p"/> This law was to apply not only to the children of Israel, but also to the stranger among them, “<hi type="italic">for</hi> (sc., it has happened) <hi type="italic">to the whole nation in mistake.</hi>” As the sin extended to the whole nation, in which the foreigners were also included, the atonement was also to apply to the whole.
entries.397e93cec8b712865be05c9d87e2055f1ff1646c: Num 15:27-29 <div eID="gen1796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1797" type="x-p"/> In the same way, again, there was one law for the native and the stranger, in relation to sins of omission on the part of single individuals. The law laid doon in <reference osisRef="Lev.5.6">Lev 5:6</reference> (cf. Lev 4:27.) for the Israelites, is repeated here in Num 15:27, Num 15:28, and in Num 15:28 it is raised into general validity for foreigners also. In Num 15:29, האזרח is written absolutely for לאזרח.
entries.9c3389b44046aabc5e41cf3abb7bc616005c0a67: Num 15:30-31 <div eID="gen1797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1798" type="x-p"/> But it was only sins committed by mistake (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference>) that could be expiated by sin-offerings. Whoever, on the other hand, whether a native or a foreigner, committed a sin “<hi type="italic">with a high hand,</hi>” - i.e., so that he raised his hand, as it were, against Jehovah, or acted in open rebellion against Him, - blasphemed God, and was to be cut off (see <reference osisRef="Gen.17.14">Gen 17:14</reference>); for he had despised the word of Jehovah, and broken His commandment, and was to atone for it with his life. בהּ עונה, “<hi type="italic">its crime upon it;</hi>” i.e., it shall come upon such a soul in the punishment which it shall endure.
entries.53132848d03cb1af140eff1cdc0bacf77822e803: Num 15:32-36 <div eID="gen1798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1799" type="x-p"/> The History of the Sabbath-Breaker is no doubt inserted here as a practical illustration of sinning “with a high hand.” It shows, too, at the same time, how the nation, as a whole, was impressed with the inviolable sanctity of the Lord’s day. From the words with which it is introduced, “<hi type="italic">and the children of Israel were in the wilderness,</hi>” all that can be gathered is, that the occurrence took place at the time when Israel was condemned to wander about in the wilderness for forty years. They found a man gathering sticks in the desert on the Sabbath, and brought him as an open transgressor of the law of the Sabbath before Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation, i.e., the college of elders, as the judicial authorities of the congregation (Exo 18:25.). They kept him in custody, like the blasphemer in <reference osisRef="Lev.24.12">Lev 24:12</reference>, because it had not yet been determined what was to be done to him. It is true that it had already been laid down in <reference osisRef="Exod.31.14-Exod.31.15">Exo 31:14-15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.35.2">Exo 35:2</reference>, that any breach of the law of the Sabbath should be punished by death and extermination, but the mode had not yet been prescribed. This was done now, and Jehovah commanded stoning (see <reference osisRef="Lev.20.2">Lev 20:2</reference>), which was executed upon the criminal without delay.
entries.d117bd65426a127eaacdb948b5867e4f4311e2bf: Num 15:37-38 (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.22.12">Deu 22:12</reference>). The command to wear Tassels on the Edge of the Upper Garment appears to have been occasioned by the incident just described. The Israelites were to wear ציצת, tassels, on the wings of their upper garments, or, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.22.12">Deu 22:12</reference>, at the four corners of the upper garment. כּסוּת, the covering in which a man wraps himself, synonymous with בּגד, was the upper garment, consisting of a four-cornered cloth or piece of stuff, which was thrown over the body-coat (see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol</hi>. ii. pp. 36, 37), and is not to be referred, as Schultz supposes, to the bed-coverings also, although this garment was actually used as a counterpane by the poor (see <reference osisRef="Exod.22.25-Exod.22.26">Exo 22:25-26</reference>). “<hi type="italic">And upon the tassel of the wing they shall put a string of hyacinth-blue,</hi>” namely, to fasten the tassel to the edge of the garment. ציצת (<hi type="italic">fem</hi>., from ציץ, the glittering, the bloom or flower) signifies something flowery or bloom-like, and is used in <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">Eze 8:3</reference> for a lock of hair; here it is applied to a tassel, as being made of twisted threads: lxx κράσπεδα; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.5">Mat 23:5</reference>, “borders.” The size of these tassels is not prescribed. The Pharisees liked to make them large, to exhibit openly their punctilious fulfilment of the law. For the Rabbinical directions how to make them, see <hi type="italic">Carpzov. apparat</hi>. pp. 197ff.; and <hi type="italic">Bodenschatz, kirchliche Verfassung der heutigen Juden,</hi> iv. pp. 11ff.
entries.a2251960bd1072e1429c6d646fd8185140c6d77c: Num 15:39-41 <div eID="gen1799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1800" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And it shall be to you for a tassel,</hi>” i.e., the fastening of the tassel with the dark blue thread to the corners of your garments shall be to you a tassel, “<hi type="italic">that ye, when ye see it, may remember all the commandments of Jehovah, and do them; and ye shall not stray after your hearts and your eyes, after which ye go a whoring</hi>.” The zizith on the sky-blue thread was to serve as a memorial sign to the Israelites, to remind them of the commandments of God, that they might have them constantly before their eyes and follow them, and not direct their heart and eyes to the things of this world, which turn away from the word of God, and lead astray to idolatry (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.25-Prov.4.26">Pro 4:25-26</reference>). Another reason for these instructions, as is afterwards added in Num 15:40, was to remind Israel of all the commandments of the Lord, that they might do them and be holy to their God, and sanctify their daily life to Him who had brought them out of Egypt, to be their God, i.e., to show Himself as God to them. Rebellion of Korah’s Company - Numbers 16:1-40(17:1-5) <div eID="gen1800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1801" type="x-p"/> The sedition of Korah and his company, with the renewed sanction of the Aaronic priesthood on the part of God which it occasioned, is the only important occurrence recorded in connection with the thirty-seven years’ wandering in the wilderness. The time and place are not recorded. The fact that the departure from Kadesh is not mentioned in Num 14, whilst, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.1.46">Deu 1:46</reference>, Israel remained there many days, is not sufficient to warrant the conclusion that it took place in Kadesh. The departure from Kadesh is not mentioned even after the rebellion of Korah; and yet we read, in Num 20:1, that the whole congregation came again into the desert of Zin to kadesh at the beginning of the fortieth year, and therefore must previously have gone away. All that can be laid down as probable is, that it occurred in one of the earliest of the thirty-seven years of punishment, though we have no firm ground even for this conjecture.  <chapter eID="Num.15"/> <div eID="gen1801" type="x-p"/>

entries.dff139d1963d3858aa70e9fef7e57c42b24a1791: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.15.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.15.1" sID="gen13366" type="section"/> <div sID="gen13367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the Lord spake.</hi> He partly here adverts to those precepts of which he had treated more distinctly and fully in Leviticus, and partly gathers into one place what he had before spoken of in various places and more obscurely. For as yet he had delivered no certain regulations as to the accessories to the meat-offering of oil and wine; but what he had before appropriated to particular cases he now commands to be observed generally, and what he had treated of more accurately he now lightly passes over; for he does not enter into full particulars, but only forbids that sacrifices should be offered without flour, a libation of wine, and oil. We have seen elsewhere that in the sacrifices and oblations, wherein God consulted the rude condition of the people, He took as it were the character of a man, as if He feasted there familiarly with them. In this sense He elsewhere calls the sacrifices His meat, <note n="291"> <div sID="gen13368" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Son pain et sa viande</foreign>;” his bread and meat. — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen13368" type="x-p"/> </note> not because He, who is the life in Himself and inspires the life of all, requires the supports of life, but because, unless He descends to men, He cannot lift up their minds to things above. Still, inasmuch as there was danger on the other side lest the people should introduce many inane and superfluous pomps, as we see that in their sacred feasts the Gentiles were foolishly and immoderately luxurious, as if their delicacies gave pleasure to God, the measure of each particular thing is prescribed, that they may not dare to invent anything arbitrarily. The conjecture is probable that what had been before delivered with sufficient clearness is here again recalled to their memory. But since this reason is not expressly given, it will be enough to hold fast what has been frequently stated, that although the ceremonies might be of trifling importance, still it was necessary that the lawful should be carefully distinguished from the unauthorized, in order that the licentiousness of men might be anticipated, who would otherwise have failed not to mingle their own leaven. The sum of this passage is, that both in the solemn sacrifices which the Law demands, as well as in the free-will-offerings, they should observe that proportion of which we have treated elsewhere.<div eID="gen13367" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.15.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen13366" osisID="Num.15.1" type="section"/>

14. And if a stranger sojourn with you. He does not mean all strangers, but only those who, descending from heathen nations, had professedly turned to God, and thus had been received into the body of the Church; for the uncleanness of those who remained in uncircumcision excluded them from the legal service. I conceive that there were two reasons why God would have one and the same form observed; first, that the proselytes who had been lately incorporated might more cheerfully devote themselves to the exercises of piety, when they saw themselves placed in the same position as the children of Abraham; and secondly, lest if any distinction should be made, corrupt mixtures should immediately creep in. Lest, therefore, the purity of God’s worship should be gradually corrupted by absurd imitation, the gate was shut against that variety which usually draws men aside in different directions.

22. And if ye have erred. He teaches by what kind of sacrifice the sins of the whole people or of each individual are to be expiated, although he enumerates only two of the four classes which are mentioned in Leviticus; for a special atonement is there enjoined both on the priest and the ruler. But neither is the ceremony of sacrificing here described, since Moses only wished to refresh their memories by the way as to the manner in which, either publicly or privately, they were to be reconciled to God. This word “error,”
“Ce mot d’inadvertence.” — Fr.
as we have said, extends to incogitancy, which partakes of contempt of God, and arises from too great security, when men inconsiderately fall into the sins to which their lusts invite them; for deliberate impiety is afterwards brought into contrast with error, when men designedly rush into violations of the law. But since nothing is more easy than for men to err, this remedy was most necessary, lest they who had sinned should fall into despair. Lest, then, the people or private individuals, when they saw their guilt, should despair of pardon and throw away the pursuit of holiness, God anticipates them, and shews them by what means He is to be propitiated, so that the sins which had occurred should not interrupt His service. Since, however, Moses here only repeats what has already been explained, there is no need of dwelling largely upon it, except that in one point he seems to deliver a law different from the former one; for he there commands two bullocks to be slain for the reconciliation of the people,
“This law differs from Leviticus 4:13, 14. Outram thinks the bullock was to be offered under that law when the whole congregation of Israel, though in other respects retaining their own rites and following the worship of the true God, yet, led away by one common error, transgressed, without knowing it, some prohibitory precept. The kid for a sin-offering, accompanied with a bullock for a burnt-offering, (see ver. 24,) Outram says he apprehends to have been required when the people, neglecting their ancient rites and unmindful of the divine laws, (which often happened under wicked kings,) were seduced into strange worship. What is recorded in 2 Chronicles 28:24, 29:3, 21, 24, Outram thinks adds much probability to his opinion. See Outram, D. 1, ch. 14, Section 2.” — Brightwell in loco.
the one as a burnt-offering, the other as a sin-offering; yet, if the second were not easily obtained, the permission was given to substitute a goat. In Leviticus, therefore, the regular and perfect rite was delivered; the permissive alteration is only added here; nor does Moses contradict himself, though, for the sake of brevity, he only refers to one of the two modes. At the end a clearer explanation is subjoined, viz., that the same law should be common to all, since it was by no means expedient to introduce any diversity.
